 By Adam Schwemley Published: 1 day ago Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, speaks during a hearing on the budget request for the EPA on Capitol Hill, Wednesday, May 13, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta) Congress returned on Nov. 9 for a lame-duck session before Democrats take control of both chambers in January. Some Republicans want to use that time to pass the SAVE America Act , a sweeping election reform bill that could change the way Americans vote in future elections.
 Sen. Lisa Murkowski has already explained why the Senate should not. She opposed the bill in a floor speech in March and again in a Wall Street Journal op-ed on July 17, where she wrote, “As written, the SAVE America Act isn’t a simple fix to safeguard elections, as proponents claim.” She supports voter ID and citizens-only voting, commonsense reforms that many of her colleagues agree with. Her concerns regarding the SAVE America Act, concerns held by many Alaskans, are about the bill’s impact on rural voting.
 The Senate version Murkowski addressed in March, a substitute amendment to Senate Bill 1383 , would require documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, including in-person presentation of that proof. Alaska has five regional election offices and a satellite office in Kenai for a state larger than Texas, California and Montana combined. Under that version, tribal IDs would qualify as voting identification only if they carry a photo and an expiration date, and Murkowski has noted that many do not. The bill includes an alternative involving an affidavit for voters unable to obtain qualifying photo ID after making reasonable efforts. More than 50,000 Alaskans voted by mail in the 2024 general election, according to Murkowski, and the March version would restrict that option. In parts of the state, incomplete records have left some Native elders without the documents the federal REAL ID law demands. Alaska began issuing REAL ID cards in January 2019, nearly 14 years after the federal law was enacted.
 Disenfranchisement may not be the bill’s intent, Murkowski told the Senate, but “I fully expect it to be an outcome of this.”
 The concern around the SAVE America Act now centers around the Senate’s calendar. A bill that could not pass in regular order all year is now being pitched as unfinished business for a departing majority, possibly through a party-line reconciliation package. But reconciliation is not an assured path around the Senate’s 60-vote threshold. Its rules restrict provisions whose budgetary effects are merely incidental to their policy changes. On June 4, an attempt to waive budget rules for a SAVE America Act amendment failed, 48-50.
 Majority Leader John Thune faces an uphill battle to secure the votes to pass a reconciliation package. Including the SAVE America Act only makes the math more difficult.
 Her vote is not in question, but one vote does not stop a bill. She should take the case she made in her floor speech and her op-ed directly to her Republican colleagues, especially those whose states share Alaska’s distances and those leaving the Senate in January who no longer face a primary. She should ask them, publicly, to join her.
 ADVERTISEMENT She is well placed to make that argument. As chair of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee, she used a March briefing on Native housing legislation to lay out what the bill would mean for Native voters. She has also argued that the Constitution largely entrusts states with administering elections and that states know their own geography best. Congress also has constitutional authority to regulate congressional elections, but that does not resolve the practical problems she has identified.
 Murkowski has said the bill does not achieve its stated goals. The remaining weeks are not enough time to repair the bill, but they are enough time for her to build the Republican opposition needed to stop it.
 Adam Schwemley is a lifelong Alaskan who currently serves as a co-director with Alaskans for Tax Reform. He lives in Wasilla.
